newsitem.title: USA: St. Louis, Mo., Mayor to review earnings tax.
newsitem.headline: St. Louis, Mo., Mayor to review earnings tax.

text.p: St. Louis, Mo., mayor-elect Clarence Harmon said Monday one of the first priorities of his new administration will be to examine the city's earnings tax.

"I have promised to do this and I will review the tax in the first 100 days of my administration," said Harmon. However, Harmon and other city officials did not outline what they would replace the the key tax with.
The city earnings tax is estimated to pump nearly $110 million into city coffers this fiscal year, or nearly a third of St. Louis' budget.
City officials, while supportive of Harmon's tax review efforts, said the tax will be hard to replace. "How do you replace more than $100 million a year?" asked city revenue collector Ron Leggett.

The issues surrounding the earnings tax took on more urgency than usual during the recent mayoral race because of a series of high profile corporate relocations out of St. Louis. Critics of the tax have said it discourages corporations from locating in St. louis.
About 65 percent of the St. Louis' earnings tax is paid by workers who live outside St. Louis and just work in the city.

St. Louis has had some form of earnings tax since the 1940s. The current tax is actually a state law and some experts warn that changing it could spark a political battle royale between state lawmakers representing the city and state lawmakers representing St. Louis' suburban interests.
"The conventional wisdom is that you don't even try to put this thing on the Capitol floor,' said former St. Louis Mayor Vincent Schoemehl Jr.
St. Louis has a budget of about $550 million this fiscal year, but about $200 million of that is earmarked for the Lambert Field airport budget.
After the earnings tax, the next two largest sources of revenue for St. Louis come from property taxes and sales taxes, which each raise about $50 million for the city annually.
